edition.locus: Octavius 39 (silence after the speech; truth adorned)
edition.license: Public domain / Latin Library as applicable

source_text: 39. Cum Octavius perorasset, aliquamdiu nos ad silentium stupefacti intentos vultus tenebamus, et quod ad me est, magnitudine admirationis evanui, quod ea, quae facilius est sentire quam dicere, et argumentis et exemplis et lectionum auctoritatibus adornasset et quod malevolos isdem illis quibus armantur, philosophorum telis retudisset, ostendisset etiam veritatem non tantummodo facilem sed et favorabilem.
pass_a_gloss: Ad silentium stupefacti. Quae facilius sentire quam dicere — argumentis, exemplis, lectionum auctoritatibus adornasset.
pass_b_english: XXXIX. When Octavius had finished speaking, for some time we, stunned to silence, held our faces intent, and as for me, I vanished in the greatness of admiration, because he had adorned with arguments and examples and authorities of readings those things which it is easier to feel than to say, and because he had refuted the malevolent with the same weapons with which they attack, and had shown both the truth of our side and the error of theirs.

lemmas.sense: easier to feel than to say

choices.choose: let argument serve what heart already feels
